extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying U.S. patent licensing and interference doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Legal rules and standards for (1) what rights pass on sale or by license of patented articles (including use, resale-price and tying restrictions) and (2) the doctrine, procedure, issues, evidence, and remedies in suits between interfering patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between property in materials and patent right to use
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between the property right in the materials composing a patented machine, and the right to use for the purpose and in the manner pointed out by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to use may be the greater element of value and is separable from title to the physical materials; a buyer may desire only some uses included in the invention. If sold unreservedly the right to the entire use passes by implied license presumed from an unconditional sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: License is not an assignment; nature of a license
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is not an assignment of any interest in the patent; it is a mere permission granted by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license may be to make, sell and use or limited to any one separable right. A license to use operates only as a right to use without being liable as an infringer; but if the licensee's use is prohibited by the license, the license is of no avail as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited permission after unauthorized manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: If a possessor manufactured a patented machine without permission and later obtains permission to use it in a particular manner or for a particular purpose, the permission carries only the right to use it in that manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title to the physical machine may at all times have belonged to the maker; permission does not convert full ownership or an unrestricted right to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: License restrictions that transcend protecting patent use may violate antitrust
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements establishing royalties, fixed prices, preferential discounts, supervisory committees, covenants to maintain prices, sales zones, and return/forfeiture schemes that control producer-to-consumer pricing transcended what was necessary to protect the use of the patent and accomplished a restraint of trade condemned by the Sherman Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts such as combining 85% of manufacturers, using a committee to fix prices, creating sales zones, requiring jobbers to sell at fixed prices, and penalties (forfeiture of royalties) indicate a scheme that 'passed to the purpose and accomplished a restraint of trade.' See Standard Sanitary Mfg. Co. v. United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to fix resale price by notice after sale is ineffective where title passed
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may not, by notice attached to sold articles, limit the price at which future retail sales of the patented articles may be made when the patentee has received the full price from an intervening purchaser (jobber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When packages are sold with full and complete title and the patentee has no further interest in proceeds or royalties, attempting to reserve the right to fix later resale prices is beyond the protection and purpose of the patent act. See Bauer v. O'Donnell; analogy to copyright 'vend'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified sale vs sale passing full title (Dick/Bobbs-Merrill distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If title is transferred but is a qualified title (e.g., right to use only with specified supplies), the patentee may retain control; conversely, an unconditional sale transfers full rights and places the article beyond the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dick case involved qualified title with use limited to specified supplies; Bauer and Bobbs-Merrill show distinctions depending on whether the sale was conditional or unconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may reserve title and impose use conditions when not a sale
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturer who reserves title to the machine and structures transactions so that complete title is not passed may impose such conditions on the right to use as he chooses, including restrictions on parts/supplies and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found elaborate notices that reserve title and restrict use (e.g., Victor Talking Machine Co. v. Straus) can be effective to avoid passing complete title; owner may give 'right to use' to various classes (distributors for demonstration, dealers, and the public) under different limitations and compensation structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of use restrictions does not depend on sale price or dependence on supply profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts in cases like Straus gave no consideration to whether the machines were sold at less than cost or whether the manufacturer depended on profit from supplies in sustaining the legitimacy of restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of such factual elements does not automatically invalidate a reserved-title restriction; the critical issue is whether title passed or was reserved and whether other statutory limits apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clayton Act §3 prohibits certain tying/conditioning that lessen competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Dick decision, the Clayton Act (Act of Oct. 15, 1914, c. 323, §3) provides that it is unlawful in commerce to make a sale on the condition that the purchaser shall not use or deal in goods of a competitor where the effect may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a restriction's effect is to 'substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly in any line of commerce,' the plan comes within the prohibition. This statutory limitation can nullify certain reserved-title/use-restriction schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying a patented machine to supplies may violate antitrust if it extends monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposing a restriction that a patented machine may only be used with films/parts manufactured by the patentee — when the patentee already monopolizes the machine market — may create a consequent monopoly in the supply market and fall within the Clayton Act or related doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion Picture Patents Co. v. Universal Film Co. held that if a patentee's machine monopoly would lead to monopoly of the film business by enforcement of the restriction, the restriction is within the Clayton prohibition; such cases may also be treated under sale/title analysis (e.g., if title passed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents interfering definition and non-coextensive claim rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents which contain one or more claims in common are interfering patents. A generic claim and an included specific claim that are not co-extensive do not interfere with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All but one of several interfering patents are necessarily void as to the interfering claim(s), though they may remain valid as to other claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of interfering claims and Commissioner's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Interfering claims may arise from Patent Office inadvertence (overlooking prior art) or because applications are filed out of chronological invention order; the Commissioner should declare an interference between an issued patent and a later application and grant a patent to the party adjudged prior inventor, but the Commissioner cannot recall a patent already granted — only courts can repeal it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference may be administrative (Patent Office) but relief from an issued patent (repeal) is a judicial function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action in equity is the prescribed proceeding for adjudicating interfering claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An action in equity is the proper proceeding to adjudicate interfering claims of issued patents in point of relative priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an action may be joined with an infringement action where complainant's patent issued first; but if defendant's patent issued first, infringement action cannot be joined with interference. Cross-bills and counterclaims have special limitations under the statute and equity practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be parties and joinder practice in interference suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant may be patentee, assignee, grantee or licensee interested in one of the patents; defendant may be patentee, assignee, grantee or licensee interested in another. It is proper to make as plaintiffs all persons who have a right and are willing, and as defendants all persons liable and found in the district; decree binds only parties and those deriving title under them after rendition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all possible parties need be joined; statute limits the effect of decrees to parties and successors after judgment; courts may enjoin transfer of a patent pending suit to preserve jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule: bill cannot be filed until complainant's patent is granted
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill in an interference suit cannot be filed until the complainant's patent is actually granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until the defendant's patent is granted there may be no occasion for such a bill; defendants may obtain affirmative relief without a cross-bill because the statute allows adjudication of patents' validity in the interference suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core questions/issues to be decided in an interference suit
rubrics_metrics.description: The key questions: (1) presence or absence of an interference; (2) whether the subject of the interference was patentable or whether either patent is void on any ground; (3) whether the first to conceive was first to reduce to practice or first to file; (4) whether the first to conceive was negligent (abandoned) before another reduced to practice or filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two may depend on claim construction and prior art; the latter two are factual and governed by rules of interference (conception, reduction to practice, diligence, abandonment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of claims is the sole test for existence of an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The interfering claims of the two patents must be substantially identical; the identity of the claims is the sole test of the existence of an interference under Section 4918.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are not substantially identical there is no jurisdiction for an interference; claim construction may be decided on demurrer only when based on the patent words alone or judicially noticeable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and admissibility in interference suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence may consist of documents, exhibits, and depositions (including those taken in Patent Office interferences) proved and supplemented by witness depositions; such Patent Office depositions are admissible according to general rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A properly authenticated copy of the Commissioner's or Court of Appeals' decision in a Patent Office interference is admissible; the Commissioner's decision is prima facie evidence in favor of the patent last granted, as is the Court of Appeals' decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of preliminary injunctions in interference suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Although injunctions are not expressly authorized by the interference statute, courts have held that a preliminary injunction can be granted in such cases under general equity powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions have been allowed historically to preserve the status quo and the equitable rights pending determination of the interference.
